source.title: Representational Similarity via Interpretable Visual Concepts
source.authors: Neehar Kondapaneni; Oisin Mac Aodha; P. Perona

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures representational similarity with interpretable concepts and regression/correlation metrics rather than the original claim's methods. It reports how similarity varies across model pairs, training conditions, and layers.
record.gate_note: The paper measures cross-model concept similarity, layerwise similarity, and effects of replacing predicted concepts on model outputs. The reported model accuracies are capability context, not measurements of representational convergence, so they are not separate rows. Hyperparameter sweeps for choosing the regression penalty and number of concepts are also not findings about the claim. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a methods paper (RSVC), but it reports how much concepts are shared across vision model pairs, seeds, training data and pretraining objectives. It uses lasso regression from one model's activations to another's concept coefficients, which is a different method aimed at the same question of shared representations. It has no scale sweep, so V1 is not really tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that RSVC reveals shared and unique visual concepts between models, and that some model differences come from unique important concepts that the other model lacks. They make no claim about universal convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses concept extraction followed by coefficient correlation or sparse lasso regression, rather than the original Platonic Representation Hypothesis measurement. It studies selected vision models and visual concepts, not broad cross-modal scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity varies by layer, similarity metric (direct correlation versus regression), architecture, training data/pretraining strategy, and concept importance. Spearman and Pearson are reported as very similar. The chosen l1 penalty and concept count affect scores, but those sweeps are presented as method-configuration analyses rather than convergence findings.
record.problems: The study is limited to computer vision models and selected model pairs. Some central outcomes are shown only in plots without exact values. Concept reconstruction error varies by model and may affect measured similarity; the authors also note that comparisons between models trained on similar datasets can be challenging.
record.rows_left_out: No results-bearing findings on the claim were omitted. Model accuracy figures were not included as rows because they do not measure representational convergence. Appendix A.13 and A.14 hyperparameter-choice results were excluded for the same reason.

untested.parts: No sweep of scale or capability. Only two size pairs (RN18/RN50, ViT-S/ViT-L) are compared, with no trend in alignment.
Entirely untested: no vision-language models and no paired image-caption data.
Stitching, relative representations and unpaired mapping. Mapping full representations rather than concept coefficients.
Neurons, SAE features and circuits recurring across many models. Language models.
Neighbour count and out-of-distribution evaluation inputs.
Plateau with scale, and whether shared data causes alignment across independently trained large models.

missing.what: Number of concepts k: increasing k disproportionately increases the number of dissimilar concepts, so measured similarity depends on a method setting.
l1 penalty λ: a higher λ reduces measured similarity (λ=0.1 vs 0.5).
Same-model similarity (SMCS) is significantly higher than cross-model similarity (CMCS), giving a ceiling against which cross-model alignment is incomplete.

record.verdict_notes: Primarily a methods paper; the convergence evidence comes from a few pairs of vision models and is mostly figure-only. The toy experiment (r1, r2) and the replacement test are method validations. The k and λ sweeps, which the reader excluded as hyperparameter choices, actually bear on V6. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Does not sweep model scale or capability systematically, and does not test convergence across arbitrary architectures, objectives, data, or modalities.
No vision-language model or paired image-caption comparison.
Tests selected same-architecture seed comparisons, not whether individual units or bases recur.
Tests sparse linear regression from activations to concept coefficients, not general lossless or low-loss mapping of full representations, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
Tests similarity between extracted visual concepts, not systematic recurrence of identified neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Tests concept-correlation and regression measures, layer, and training-data/model choices; does not vary neighbour count or test out-of-distribution inputs as a metric-dependence condition.
Tests selected training data, seeds, and pretraining differences; does not isolate shared training data or objectives as causal explanations for similarity.

rows.subject: Mnc → Mps (ResNet-18 models)
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch on modified NABirds
rows.operation_detail: Measured concept similarity for Mps Concept 1, visually identified as the pink-square concept.
rows.note: Mnc was trained with the pink square made non-predictive; the authors report near-zero similarity to the pink-square concept learned by Mps.
rows.check: Designed validation. Mnc was trained to ignore the pink square on purpose, so the near-zero similarity is an induced difference, not evidence on convergence.

rows.subject: Mnc → Mps (ResNet-18 models)
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch on modified NABirds
rows.operation_detail: Measured similarity for two other Mps concepts after toy-concept training.

conditions.value: Concepts 2 and 3; bird colour pattern and water background

rows.value: figure only; described as very high similarity
rows.note: The paper says these two shared concepts were unaffected by training on the pink-square concept; exact scores are not given in the text.
rows.check: Specificity check for the toy experiment. It validates the method rather than testing convergence.

rows.subject: RN18 vs. RN50; RN50 vs. ViT-S; ViT-S vs. ViT-L; DINO vs. MAE
rows.size_stated: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-S, ViT-L, DINO ViT-B, MAE ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet-trained; DINO and MAE fine-tuned on NABirds
rows.operation_detail: Measured penultimate-layer cross-model concept similarity and concept importance.

conditions.value: four model pairs listed in the subject

rows.measure: Cross-model concept similarity (CMCS) and concept importance
rows.value: Most concepts have medium/high similarity, with dense regions above 0.6; low/medium-similarity concepts with medium/high importance occur in all comparisons except DINO vs. MAE.
rows.note: The results include both shared concepts and important concepts that one model predicts poorly. The text describes patterns across the four pairs rather than reporting pairwise summary statistics.
rows.check: Drop V1: there is no scale trend, only four fixed pairs. Dense regions are above 0.6, but unique low-similarity, high-importance concepts exist in three of the four pairs.

rows.subject: RN18 vs. RN50
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept coefficients across selected layer pairs using maximum Pearson correlation.
rows.value: figure only; highest in early layers, declines with depth, and rises slightly toward the final layers
rows.note: The text describes the layerwise pattern; exact layer-pair scores are only plotted.
rows.check: Drop V1 and V4: this is a correlation measure (MMCS), not a mapping. MMCS values are roughly 0.2–0.6 and decay with depth, so the effect depends on layer.

rows.subject: ViT-S vs. ViT-L
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept coefficients across selected layer pairs using maximum Pearson correlation.
rows.value: figure only; similarity is higher for ViT-S layers 4–9 against ViT-L layers 5–20, with a rise between the last ViT-S layer and the last three ViT-L layers
rows.note: The text reports a layer-dependent pattern rather than a single overall score.
rows.check: Drop V1 and V4. The pattern is layer-dependent and MMCS is about 0.2–0.45.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.1.2; Figure A1: ViT-S layers 4–9 versus ViT-L layers 5–20

rows.subject: RN50 vs. ViT-S

rows.value: figure only; ResNet-50 layers 0–25 are most similar to ViT-S layers 0–3
rows.note: The reported correspondence is between different relative depths in the two architectures.
rows.check: Drop V1 and V4. Correspondence is between different relative depths of the two architectures.

rows.subject: MAE vs. DINO

rows.subject: Four model pairs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-S, ViT-L, DINO ViT-B, MAE ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet-trained; DINO and MAE fine-tuned on NABirds
rows.operation_detail: Compared direct coefficient correlations with sparse lasso regression followed by Pearson correlation.
rows.value: CMCS is correlated with MCS and usually gives higher similarity; the authors describe MCS as a noisy lower bound.
rows.note: The reported comparison aggregates plotted concept-level results across the four model pairs.
rows.check: Drop V4. Direct correlation (MCS) gives systematically lower similarity than regression (CMCS), so measured similarity depends on the measure.

rows.subject: Four model pairs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-S, ViT-L, DINO ViT-B, MAE ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet-trained; DINO and MAE fine-tuned on NABirds
rows.operation_detail: Replaced concept coefficients with cross-model predicted coefficients and measured changes in activations, logits, and predictions.

conditions.value: Pearson correlation change and concept importance

rows.measure: Activation L2 distance, logit KL divergence, and prediction match accuracy
rows.value: As similarity decreases, activation L2 distance and KL divergence increase and prediction match accuracy decreases; low-importance concepts have no effect on KL divergence.
rows.note: The paper says these trends roughly hold across models, though plot structure differs for ViTs. The figure contains the numeric points.
rows.check: Drop V1, V5 and V6. The replacement test shows that low-similarity, important concepts mapped cross-model change logits and predictions, so the mapping is not lossless.

rows.subject: DINO vs. MAE (NABirds)
rows.operation_detail: Replacement test using cross-model predicted concept coefficients.

conditions.value: Pearson correlation change; activation distance, logit KL divergence, prediction match

rows.measure: Activation L2 distance, logit KL divergence, and prediction match accuracy
rows.value: As Pearson correlation decreases, L2 distance and KL divergence increase, and match accuracy decreases; smaller correlation changes produce behavior changes on the same order as the other comparisons.
rows.note: The authors say DINO and MAE appear more sensitive to concept changes; the cause is unclear.
rows.check: Drop V1, V5 and V6. DINO and MAE are more sensitive to small similarity drops.

rows.subject: DINO s483 vs. DINO s873
rows.stage_stated: Fine-tuned on NABirds with different seeds
rows.operation_detail: Compared layerwise and average concept similarity across seed variants.
rows.baseline: DINO s483 compared with MAE s483: ∼0.80
rows.note: The text says individual concepts change with seed, while the global relationship between the models is preserved.
rows.check: Drop V5, V6 and V7. The DINO seed pair has ∼0.89 average similarity; the 0.80 DINO-vs-MAE value is a comparison, not a baseline.

rows.subject: DINO s873 vs. MAE s873
rows.stage_stated: Fine-tuned on NABirds with seed 87363356; different pretraining strategies
rows.operation_detail: Compared average concept similarity across the two pretraining strategies.
rows.note: The average similarity is reported in both directions; the paper says the layerwise relationship resembles the other seed comparison.
rows.check: Drop V1 and V6. A different pretraining objective lowers average similarity to ∼0.80, against ∼0.89 across seeds.

rows.subject: DINO vs. MAE (NABirds)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Pearson correlation and sparse-regression concept similarity.
rows.value: Spearman results were very similar to Pearson results; Spearman results were omitted from the paper.
rows.note: This is the only explicit text comparison of Pearson and Spearman outcomes.
rows.check: Applies to all experiments, not only DINO vs MAE. Spearman and Pearson give very similar results, so there is no dependence on the choice between these two correlations.

relation.reason: The paper reports its own measurements of shared and unique concepts, mapping fidelity, layer dependence and training dependence.

tranche.reason: Concept extraction, coefficient correlation and sparse regression provide a different method for testing shared representations across architectures, seeds and training protocols.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. Similarity depends on concept extraction and reconstruction error; DINO seed comparisons vary fine-tuning seeds, and the waterbird ablation retrains the head on the full dataset.

statements.correction: 169 waterbird classes excluded during backbone training; backbone then frozen; classification head trained on full NABirds; accuracy 25% versus 34%; only a slight increase in dissimilar concepts relative to seed variation; no disjoint-training-data test.
statements.problem: The slight-change result is accurate, but this study does not establish that shared training examples are unnecessary: the backbone datasets overlap, and the classification head is subsequently trained on all NABirds classes.
